body:
Thanks - focusing on the different behavior when running as a script vs running inside Jupyter (for the proposed interface change, please see #2778).

When running the attached script, does the script exit right after the printing of:
```
Job ID: <hidden>
```
with no extra delay?

I can reproduce that behavior locally: and it seems it can be explained at least partially due to timing. As the script exits almost immediately, the underlying `future` (created [here](https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit/blob/main/qiskit/primitives/primitive_job.py#L54-L56)) likely does not have time to start running, which leads to graceful shutdown as the script ends. Can you try adding a `sleep(1)` after the `print` statement, and comment back on the script and notebook behavior? Locally (and testing on the script), that extra time makes the `future` able to start running - so the script execution does not end until the simulator execution ends.

I'm also wondering about the use case: you are creating a `job`, but not waiting for it to finish (usually via `job.result()`). Waiting for the result to be available would ensure your "session" (as in, the script or the notebook) is alive until the simulation is completed.

Hi Diego, Thanks for getting back on the issue, I tried adding `sleep(1)` and `sleep(5)` after the print statements and the resultant behavior is very stochastic in both. Most of the times it results in `segmentation fault` or `double free or corruption`, very few times it also spawned the processes and started the simulation which required killing the process to stop (same as notebook) but this is very random.

Since the behavior still seems stochastic, what do you think would be the best fix for this ? Ideally, my first thought was if QEM is not allowed on the simulators and fakebackends, it should not go through with the execution at all since user might expect mitigated value but they get a noisy value, if the warnings are ignored or not understood well.

The second potential fix can be - "Fixing it upstream in qiskit core, Make `PrimitiveJob._submit` use a daemon worker", as I mentioned in the suggested solutions in the issue description.

Regarding the usecase, I was working on analysing the quantum error mitigation techniques along with simulators when I noticed this issue.

Thanks for checking - at a first look, it does seem to point to an out of memory issue. Simulators are very demanding in terms of memory (you can find more details in [this documentation page](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/debugging-tools)), with tight correlation with the number of qubits (and it seems you are using `ibm_kingston`, which is a 156 qubit device), and your job might just be too demanding (for the record, locally when I added the extra delay for ensuring the simulator has enough time to kick in and the `future` to start running, I did not wait for the job to finish, killed the process).

A suggestion for approaching validating and debugging using simulators would be to try to start with a simpler version of the problem (as hinted in the linked documentation page: smaller circuits if applicable, smaller devices if applicable), and scale up to the full version of the problem using a real device. Regardless, you will always find simulators useful for just a subset of purposes (they don't provide the same features as a real device as you experienced, and are not practical for large workloads), and you are bound to hit some limits inherent to simulators - so when designing an experiment, it is usually worth to plan around the differences between simulator and devices accordingly.

Other suggestions that might help:
* you might find the [fake providers](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/api/qiskit-ibm-runtime/fake-provider) convenient for your needs. In general, we encourage using them instead of an `AerSimulator` instance directly. It adds a few layers in between when it comes to submission, but might streamline your workflow.
* if you suspect the segmentation fault / double free or corruption might come from a `qiskit-aer` bug, I would encourage coming up with a simpler reproducible example and inspecting the core dump, and reaching out to Aer maintainers throw an issue in their repo.
* a (sketchy) look into what happens when using `Estimator.run()` with a simulator backend is:
   1. `qiskit_ibm_runtime.fake_provider.local_service.QiskitRuntimeService::_run_backend_primitive_v2()` is the last layer in this package that is responsible for signalling that the job is to be run
   2. `qiskit.primitives.backend_estimator_v2.BackendEstimatorV2::run()` creates and submits the job, ultimately running `qiskit.primitives.backend_estimator_v2._run_circuits()` inside a `future`
   3. if using a `FakeBackend`, `qiskit_ibm_runtime.fake_provider.fake_backend.FakeBackendV2::run()` is invoked, which delegates into `AerSimulator` 
   4. `qiskit_aer.backends.aer_simulator.AerSimulator::run()` performs the actual simulation

   This is mostly a pointer for pieces that might help diagnose further or provide you with more control. As technical notes, `future`s are usually [not cancellable](https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html#concurrent.futures.Future.cancel) once they start running and are integral part of the current approach - which makes changing the overall model quite involved.

I still wonder about the specific of the use case (thanks for the insight!): if you are not making use of the result of the job, I wonder if you do need to create a job at all in your scenario (which would bypass the need for graceful termination or memory issues). Pretty much all the workflows assume that if an user is submitting a job (locally or remotely), that job will be waited for and the results used one way or the other (so keeping the script or notebook until a job is completed, and managing the job complexity and ensuring it can be simulated in the user local environment are in practice delegated to the user domain) - supporting such an edge use case might be outside scope.
